 Steve Smith is a national hero, owned Sandpapergate without blaming others: Ex-teammate
 Moises Henriques believes Steve Smith took the fall for Sandpapergate despite opposing the plan, calling him a national hero. His comments came after Cameron Bancroft, who tampered with the ball in 2018, claimed Smith did not approve of their plan in the dressing room in Cape Town.
 Advertisement Steve Smith was banned for a year for his role in ball-tampering scandal in 2018. Courtesy: Reuters/Getty Images By: India Today Sports Desk New Delhi , Nov 19, 2026 15:29 IST Last Updated Nov 19, 2026 15:29 IST Published by Akshay Ramesh Nov 19, 2026 15:29 IST Former Australia all-rounder Moises Henriques has called Steve Smith a national hero, saying the former captain took responsibility for the 2018 ball-tampering scandal despite not wanting any part of the plan, as revealed by Cameron Bancroft in his latest account of Sandpapergate.
 Bancroft, who was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Cape Town Test in March 2018, claimed in a lengthy account published on Wednesday that Smith had distanced himself from the plan when it was discussed. According to Bancroft, Smith did not approve of the idea and wanted out of the situation. Yet, when the scandal erupted, Smith stood alongside Bancroft at the press conference, accepted responsibility and did not publicly implicate other members of the team.
 advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story Henriques believes that decision is what sets Smith apart, arguing that the former Australia captain could have named those involved but chose to protect his teammates.
 "There's the Australian cricket captain, in front of the coach, in front of the assistant coach, in front of the vice-captain of the time, in front of other people, saying 'I don't approve', and walking away from it," Henriques said on the Cricket Fanatics podcast alongside former Test players Stuart MacGill and Steve O'Keefe.
 "He could have easily thrown people under the bus ... but you know what he did? He went out in that press conference with Bangers, and he owned it.
 "He's owned it on behalf of his team, and then after this, he's not flinging mud at anyone.
 "He doesn't want any of the bowlers to pay. He doesn't want anyone to pay.
 "I'm sure he knows a lot more stuff - to me, he's a national hero out of all of this."
 Henriques' comments add another layer to the debate over the roles played by Australia's senior players in the scandal. Bancroft's account came after former opener Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr, in which he also suggested that the knowledge of the ball-tampering plan extended beyond the three players who were sanctioned. Australia captain Pat Cummins subsequently rejected the suggestion that the entire team was aware of the plan during a press conference, prompting further discussion around the episode. CLARKE HAS A DIFFERENT VIEW
 Former Australia captain Michael Clarke, however, believes Smith still had a responsibility to act, regardless of whether he approved of the plan.
 Speaking on the Beyond23 Cricket Podcast, Clarke acknowledged that Smith had taken the punishment and returned to the game, but said the responsibility of leadership could not be separated from what happened.
 "As captain, you always stand tall. As a leader, that is your responsibility," Clarke said.
 "Leadership under pressure is the hardest thing in the world. But that is what this team, Cricket Australia, this game needs right now.
 "Steve Smith did stand there and take the hit, served his punishment and come back.
 advertisement "It sounds like, if I believe what Cam's (Bancroft) written and what Uzzie's (Usman Khawaja) written and other people have said, Smitty didn't want to know about it, but he knew about it.
 "So as captain, there is still a responsibility."
 Smith was handed a 12-month ban and removed as Australia captain following the scandal. He is yet to speak to the press again since Bancroft's latest revelations.
 Cricket Australia has since announced a forum for players and staff from the 2018 tour to share their recollections, while ruling out a formal reinvestigation. With Bancroft's account reopening questions about what happened in Cape Town, Henriques and Clarke have offered contrasting perspectives on Smith's role: one focused on his decision not to implicate teammates, the other on the responsibility he carried as captain. - Ends Must Watch
